subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography - Rivers
subtitle: Reading passages for KS3 river systems and flood geography.
description: A KS3 geography revision pack on how rivers work from source to mouth. It covers drainage basins, downstream change, river processes, landforms, flooding, flood management, case studies and fieldwork data skills.

data.sourcePassage: A river is part of a drainage basin system. The drainage basin is the area of land drained by the main river and its tributaries. The watershed is the high boundary around the basin. Rainfall can move through the system in different ways. Some water flows across the surface as surface runoff, while some soaks into the ground by infiltration before moving slowly through soil and rock. The shape of the basin, rock type, land use, vegetation and recent weather all affect how quickly water reaches the channel. A common mistake is to confuse a tributary with a confluence. A tributary is the smaller river; a confluence is the exact point where two rivers meet.

data.sourcePassage: Rivers usually change from source to mouth. Near the source, the upper course often has a steep gradient, a narrow channel and a V-shaped valley. Downstream, tributaries add more water, so discharge usually increases. The channel commonly becomes wider and deeper, and sediment tends to become smaller and rounder because of attrition. The long profile becomes gentler towards the mouth, while cross profiles show wider valleys and deeper channels. It is important not to say that rivers only erode in the upper course and only deposit in the lower course. Erosion, transportation and deposition can happen anywhere, although some processes are more common in certain sections.

data.sourcePassage: Waterfalls often form where a river flows over hard rock and soft rock. The softer rock erodes more quickly by hydraulic action and abrasion, creating a step and a plunge pool. The hard rock is left as an overhang, but this overhang eventually becomes unsupported and collapses. The collapsed rock can scrape the plunge pool and make it deeper. Over time, the waterfall retreats upstream and leaves behind a narrow, steep-sided gorge. Meanders form in a different part of the river system. On the outside bend, water flows faster and erosion undercuts the bank. On the inside bend, water is slower and deposition creates a slip-off slope. If the neck of a meander is cut through and the old bend is sealed by deposition, an oxbow lake forms.

data.sourcePassage: Flooding happens when water covers land that is normally dry. River floods often occur when discharge becomes too high for the channel to hold. Heavy rainfall matters, but it is rarely the only cause. Saturated ground, impermeable rock, steep slopes and narrow valleys can all make water reach the river quickly. Human activity can also increase flood risk. Urbanisation creates roads, roofs and car parks that reduce infiltration and increase surface runoff. Deforestation reduces interception, so more rain reaches the ground quickly. A hydrograph helps geographers understand this response by showing rainfall and river discharge over time. The time between peak rainfall and peak discharge is called lag time.

data.sourcePassage: Flood management aims to reduce flood risk or reduce the impact of floods. Hard engineering uses built structures such as dams, flood walls, embankments, channel straightening and flood relief channels. These can give strong protection, especially in valuable urban areas, but they can be expensive and may damage habitats or move flood risk downstream. Soft engineering works more with natural processes. Examples include flood warnings, floodplain zoning, tree planting, river restoration, wetlands and permeable surfaces. These methods can be cheaper and more sustainable, but they may need land and may not stop the largest floods. A strong flood plan often combines methods rather than relying on one solution.

data.sourcePassage: Boscastle in Cornwall experienced a severe flash flood on 16 August 2004. Very heavy rainfall fell in a short time, the drainage basin was steep, and the ground became saturated. Two rivers, the Valency and Jordan, meet near the village, which increased flood risk, and the narrow valley helped funnel water through the settlement. Cars were swept away, homes and businesses were damaged, roads and bridges were affected, and people had to be rescued, including by helicopter. After the flood, the river channel was widened in places, a new bridge design reduced blockage by debris, and flood walls and drainage were improved. The case study shows that flooding is caused by a combination of weather, basin characteristics and human vulnerability.

data.sourcePassage: Geographers use fieldwork to investigate how rivers change downstream. At several safe sites, students might measure width with a tape measure, depth with a metre ruler, velocity by timing a float over a measured distance, and sediment size with a ruler or callipers. To calculate average depth, they add several depth readings and divide by the number of readings. Fieldwork has limitations. A float may only show surface velocity, sediment samples may be too small, and results collected on one day may not represent normal conditions. Reliability improves when students repeat measurements, use the same method at each site, choose several sites downstream, and record recent weather. Safety matters, so students should avoid deep or fast water and work with adult supervision.
